The simplex as its own shape

Hypercube Composition Theory. The triangle and its higher versions, set up in their own polar coordinates and compared with the cube and the hypersphere. Blue in the pictures is the simplex, orange the sphere, grey the cube.

The simplex as its own shape (DRAFT)

DRAFT, Nov 26 2026. Part of Hypercube Composition Theory (repo: fused-hyperoperation-algebra). Asked for by Brennan: "let's look at the simplex as well. And use that as another shape that we try to do things with." Builds on polar-coordinates/ and polar-recast/ and does not repeat them. Checks: checks.py → checks_output.txt, 44 of 44 pass (numpy, scipy); section 7 (cubic-form dial) adds 26 of 26. Pictures: figures.py → figures/. No Lean in this pass (no Lean on this machine). Colour key: blue = the simplex / our readings, orange = the sphere, grey = the cube.

The result in four sentences

The simplex (the triangle, tetrahedron and their higher versions, every list of shares that adds to 1) is the shape of a fixed total, and our operation lives on it in two places: at k = −1 it is stick-breaking, which turns the cube into the simplex, and at k = +1 it is Bayes' rule, which moves you around inside it. The simplex gives e most simply (its corner volumes 1/n! add to e), it only borrows π from the sphere (through square roots), and it has no i at all: it is exactly the sphere with its phases forgotten, which is the Born rule. The sharpest comparison is with the sphere: one distance rule (Hilbert's) makes the ball into relativity's velocity space, which is curved and precesses, and makes the simplex into a flat space where updates commute and nothing precesses. In one dimension the two agree exactly: a coin's log odds is a rapidity. Update (section 7): the shape itself is a second dial, separate from the curvature dial (the plane dial). Sliding from round to triangle fades the leftover turn from −1 to 0, it becomes a pattern across the shape in between, and cooling is one route along this dial.

Figure 9. Which shape each family belongs to. The simplex column is every law with a fixed total.

1. Polar coordinates on the simplex: three coordinate systems on one triangle

Figure 1. Left: the cube of stick fractions (v₁, v₂). Middle: the triangle of probabilities, with the cube's grid (blue) and the sphere's angle grid (orange dashed) drawn on it. Right: the octant of the sphere, where the amplitudes √p live. Squaring sends the sphere onto the triangle; stick-breaking sends the cube onto it.

One point of the simplex can be written three ways:

Coordinates What they are Where they come from
Barycentric p₁ … pₙ (sum 1) the shares themselves the simplex itself
Stick fractions v₁ … vₙ₋₁ in [0,1] "take v of what's left" at each cut the cube, via our law at k = −1
Angles θ₁ … θₙ₋₁ in [0, π/2] hyperspherical angles of √p the sphere, via squaring

and they are tied together by v = cos²θ (check S3). So stick-breaking is the polar coordinate system of the simplex: each cut is one angle.

Ours (on known math): the running total of the pieces is v₁ ∘₋₁ v₂ ∘₋₁ … ∘₋₁ vₘ (check S1), because what is left after each cut multiplies: 1 − (a ∘₋₁ b) = (1 − a)(1 − b). The map is one-to-one from the open cube onto the open simplex (S2), and the even spread on the simplex comes from independent Beta(1, n − m) cuts (S4). Known: stick-breaking (Sethuraman 1994, the Dirichlet process), hyperspherical coordinates.

Figure 2. Breaking a stick four times. The running total after each cut is the core law at k = −1 applied to the fractions taken.

Verdict: a real bridge, not a new theorem. It says the cube and the simplex are two coordinate charts of one thing, joined by our own operation, and that the sphere's angles are a third chart of the same thing.

2. One dial, three jobs on the simplex

Figure 3. k = −1 builds the simplex from the cube (even cuts land unevenly). k = 0 adds the shares of outcomes that can't happen together. k = +1 is Bayes' rule: repeated evidence bends across the triangle but is a straight line of equal steps in log-ratio coordinates.

  • k = −1, builds. Stick-breaking (section 1).
  • k = 0, adds. Shares of outcomes that exclude each other just add. That is the budget region of the beyond-the-cube pass at k = 0.
  • k = +1, moves. Bayes' rule multiplies each share by a likelihood and renormalizes (Aitchison's "perturbation"). The odds against the last outcome, rᵢ = pᵢ/pₙ, multiply, so rᵢ − 1 composes by ∘₁ (check R1). The simplex's own radius coordinate, the log-ratio log(pᵢ/pₙ), is our ruler L₁ applied to odds − 1 (R2). Repeated identical evidence is equal steps along a straight line in those coordinates (R3).

Known: Aitchison's geometry of compositions (1982–86), Bayes in odds form. The project already knew that the flip φ₋₁(x) = x/(1 − x) is the odds and carries ∘₋₁ to ∘₁. Ours: reading the three dial settings as build / add / move on one shape. Verdict: unifies; no new theorem.

3. The simplex and the sphere: square roots and forgotten phases

Figure 4. Random complex amplitudes, squared, spread evenly over the simplex (Archimedes' hat-box). Random real amplitudes (no phase) pile up at the edges, the arcsine law.

  • Square roots make the simplex round. The natural statistical distance on the simplex (Fisher's) is twice the angle between √p and √q: the simplex is one corner of a sphere of radius 2 (checks F2, F3).
  • Forgetting phases lands on the simplex. A random point on the complex sphere, squared, is spread perfectly evenly over the simplex (F4). That is Archimedes' hat-box theorem in its general form, and it is the Born rule: probabilities are the sphere of amplitudes with every phase thrown away. With real amplitudes (no phase), the shares crowd the edges with density 1/(π√(p(1 − p))) (F5).
  • Lévy's arcsine law for random walks is the same picture: the fraction of time a walk spends ahead has a uniform simplex angle (F6).

Known: Fisher/Rao/Bhattacharyya; Wootters 1981 (statistical distance = angle between states, F7); Archimedes; the moment map of complex projective space onto the simplex; Lévy 1939. Ours: nothing new; this section is the bridge that lets us compare the simplex with the hypersphere page.

4. Constants: e lives here, π is borrowed, i is absent

Figure 5. Left: the corner simplex of the unit n-cube has volume 1/n!, and these add up to e. Second: the cube is n! such simplices, one for each ordering of its coordinates. Third: volumes summed over every dimension: corner simplex e, cross-polytope e², ball e^π(1 + erf √π) ≈ 46.0, cube infinite. Right: squaring bends the coin's segment into a quarter circle, and its Fisher length is π.

  • e. The corner simplex of the unit n-cube has volume 1/n! (E1); the cube splits into n! of them, one per ordering (E2); the volumes add to e (E3). Scaled by t, they add to eᵗ (E6): the simplex is the shape of the exponential. The average count of random numbers needed to pass 1 is e (E4). The e page's layers C(n,k)/nᵏ → 1/k! are exactly these volumes (E5). Simpler on the simplex: yes. On the cube every volume is 1 and the sum diverges; on the sphere the sum is e^π(1 + erf √π), true but not simpler.
  • π. The simplex has no π of its own. π appears only after square roots turn it into a piece of sphere: the coin's Fisher length is π (F1), the Fisher volume of the simplex is half the sphere's area (F3), the arcsine law's 1/π (F5). Simpler on the sphere.
  • i. Absent. The simplex is what is left of the sphere after the phases (the i's) are forgotten (F4). Lives on the sphere only.

Known: all of these facts. Ours: the three-way sorting, and the line from the e page to the corner simplices.

5. One distance rule, three shapes (the main comparison)

Figure 6. Hilbert's distance (half the log of a cross-ratio with the two boundary points on the line) drawn as balls of radius 0.25, 0.5 and 0.8 around three centres. Triangle: hexagons, all alike in log-ratio coordinates (flat). Disk: hyperbolic geometry (curved). Square: the balls change shape as they move.

Hilbert's distance needs only a convex shape, so it is a fair way to compare shapes.

  • Segment. Distance from the middle is the rapidity, and Einstein's velocity addition, our plane law at k = 0, d = −1, adds it (H1).
  • Ball. It is hyperbolic space in the Klein model (H6), which is exactly the space of velocities in special relativity.
  • Simplex. It is half the spread of the log-ratios (H3); Bayes updates are distance-preserving shifts (H4); tempering a belief by t multiplies its distance by t (H5). So it is a flat normed space, with hexagonal balls.
  • Square. Not flat and not a product of the two axis rapidities (H10, H11).

Known: Klein model; Foertsch and Karlsson 2005 proved that the simplex is the only convex shape whose Hilbert geometry is a normed space; de la Harpe 1993 for the hexagonal balls.

Relativity precesses, Bayes does not

Figure 7. Left: two perpendicular velocities of 0.8c composed in either order end 28.1° apart (Thomas–Wigner rotation). Middle: two pieces of evidence taken in either order land on the same belief; the loop closes. Right: the leftover turn equals the area of the velocity triangle, for 150 random cases.

  • On the ball, u ⊕ v and v ⊕ u differ by the Wigner angle arccos((γᵤ + γᵥ)/(1 + γᵤγᵥ)) (H7), and that angle is exactly the area of the hyperbolic triangle 0, u, u ⊕ v (H8). That is our precession page's swap rule, turn = d × area, with d = −1.
  • On the simplex, Bayes updates commute exactly (H9). No area, no turn.

Figure 8. Left: in one dimension, 0.5c ⊕ 0.6c = 0.846c and "odds ×3 then ×4 = odds 12" are the same two steps on one line (rapidity = ½ log odds, H2). Middle: temperature turns a round ball into the simplex (free-energy level sets, R5). Right: the polar pass's ℓp dial (the roundness dial) for comparison.

  • In one dimension they are the same law (H2): put p = (1 + v)/2, and the odds (1 + v)/(1 − v) multiply exactly when velocities add Einstein's way. The identity is elementary; I found no source stating it, so treat the observation as likely noticed before.
  • In two or more dimensions they split by shape: round velocity space curves and precesses, flat belief space doesn't.

Ours: putting relativity and Bayes side by side as the ball and the simplex under one rule, and placing the Thomas angle on our swap-rule line. Known: each half (Rhodes and Semon 2004 for Thomas rotation as hyperbolic area; Foertsch–Karlsson for the simplex).

6. Laws that come out simpler on the simplex

Law On the simplex Check
Bayes' rule a straight shift (∘₁ on odds − 1), distance-preserving R1–R3, H4
Gibbs / softmax temperature slides from the centre (hot) to a corner (cold) R4
Roundness hot free-energy ball is a sphere, cold one is the simplex R5
Entropy its curvature is the Fisher metric R6
Replicator equation (biology) the Fisher-metric uphill direction of mean fitness R7
Born rule sphere with phases forgotten, lands evenly F4
Arcsine law uniform in the simplex angle F6
Conservation (mass, charge, probability) the total is the simplex's defining equation (definition)
Corner-weight shapes every one is a weighted sum of simplices (Postnikov) polar pass E1

Harder or no help on the simplex: relativity and precession (need the ball), i and π (need the sphere), independent events (need the cube), number theory (torus of angles), Navier–Stokes, Newton's G and Fermat (unchanged).

7. The cubic-form dial (the shape dial): a second dial, separate from the curvature dial

Asked for by Brennan after the first pass: hold the curvature dial fixed, slide the shape from round to triangle, and see whether the law still changes; and test whether the leftover turn fades smoothly as temperature drops. Checks: shape_dial.py (method) and shape_dial_checks.py → shape_dial_checks_output.txt, 26 of 26 pass. Pictures: figures_shape_dial.py → figures/fig10 … fig13.

Result. Yes, it is a separate dial. With the curvature dial held fixed, sliding the shape from round to triangle moves the leftover turn per unit area from the full Thomas amount (−1) to nothing (0), smoothly and in one direction, along every route tried. In between, the turn is no longer one number: it varies from place to place inside the shape, and no setting of the curvature dial can do that, because the curvature dial only scales the turn evenly. Cooling does the same thing: the turn fades smoothly to zero, about 1.45/β when cold, with no jump.

Figure 10. Curvature dial fixed, shape sliding from round to triangle. Colour is the turn per unit area at each point (orange = the full Thomas turn, blue = none). The round end turns the same everywhere; in between, the rounded corners still turn while the flat sides stop; the triangle turns nowhere.

How the turn is measured on a shape that is neither. Every convex shape has one distance rule that its own projective symmetries keep (Vinberg's characteristic function: the area of the "polar" shape seen from each point, log of it, second derivatives, minus a third of the square of the first). On the round shape this is relativity's velocity space; on the triangle it is the flat Bayes space of section 5. The leftover turn around a small loop is the curvature of this rule times the loop's area (Gauss–Bonnet), which is exactly how the Thomas–Wigner turn arises on the round shape. I report the curvature scaled so the round shape gives −1 (written K̂). Checks V1–V5 confirm the method: −1 on the disk at every point and every size, 0 on the triangle, and the polar-area formula matches the exact one.

  • Two routes, same answer (M1–M3, C1). Blending disk into triangle gives centre values −1, −0.89, −0.63, −0.32, 0; trimming the triangle with a disk gives −1, −0.95, −0.76, −0.50, −0.24, −0.07, 0. Halfway along the blend the value runs from −0.82 near a rounded corner to −0.50 near a flat side.
  • Temperature (T1–T5). The free-energy shapes of Figure 8 run from round (hot) to triangle (cold). The centre value goes −0.9996, −0.997, −0.965, −0.69, −0.37, −0.14, −0.048, −0.015, −0.005, −0.0014 for β = 0.001 to 1000: about −1 + 0.35β when hot and −1.45/β when cold. So the temperature dial is a route along the cubic-form dial, and the leftover turn fades with it. The earlier lead (section 5, lead 1) passes its test.
  • Only the triangle is flat (P1–P12, L-checks). Squares, pentagons, hexagons, any regular polygon with four or more sides, and the ℓᵖ balls all look perfectly round at their centre (K̂ = −1) and flatten toward their edges. The triangle is the only one flat at its centre.
  • Always between the two ends (B1). 262 points in 45 random shapes (30 polygons, 15 smooth blobs) all gave −1 ≤ K̂ ≤ 0. So round and triangle are the two extremes of this dial, not two stops among many.

Figure 11. Left: the centre turn along two different routes from round to triangle. Right: cooling the free-energy shape; dashed and dotted lines are the cold and hot rates.

Why it is not the curvature dial. The curvature dial d is the overall scale: on the round shape it sets c (d = −1/c²), and the turn per unit velocity-area is |d| × K̂, the same at every point. Turning d down to zero gives Galileo: flat, but with round unit balls. The triangle is flat with hexagonal unit balls (de la Harpe; Foertsch–Karlsson). So the two dials reach "no turn" at two different places, and on the triangle the curvature dial changes nothing about the turn at all. One more difference: an addition law (a group of moves that carries every point to every other) exists only at the two ends. Round has the three-dimensional Lorentz group, whose boosts don't commute, and the commutator is the Thomas turn; the triangle has a two-dimensional group of scalings, which commute. Every shape in between has only finitely many symmetries (Benzécri; in the plane, ellipse and triangle are the only shapes with symmetries that reach every point). So between the ends the "law" survives only as the turn field, not as an addition rule.

Figure 12. The two dials side by side. Colour is the centre turn rate |d| × |K̂| (schematic in the shape direction, using the blend route). Up and down scales the turn evenly; left to right changes its pattern and ends at a place, flat with hexagonal balls, that the curvature dial never reaches.

Figure 13. Left: centre turn rate for regular polygons; only the triangle is flat there. Right: the square is round in the middle and flatter near its edges.

The right name. The dial is the space of convex shapes up to projective change (Benzécri's space; each shape carries its own Hilbert geometry). The quantity that measures, point by point, how far a shape has moved from round toward cornered is a cubic form: for surfaces, the Pick cubic form, or the cubic differential of Labourie and Loftin. It is zero exactly for ellipses (Pick–Berwald), and Dumas–Wolf picture the triangle as the extreme case.

One caveat on the numbers. A convex shape has two standard symmetric distance rules: Vinberg's, which I computed, and the Blaschke (Cheng–Yau) metric, which is the one the Pick form and the cubic differential belong to. Both give −1 on round shapes and 0 on the triangle, and both have curvature set by a cubic third-derivative term, but they differ in between, so the in-between values depend on which you pick. The verdict (separate dial, smooth fade, ends at −1 and 0) does not. For the Blaschke metric the −1 to 0 range is Calabi's bound, which I recall but did not find confirmed in the searches here; for Vinberg's metric it held at every point tested, which is a numerical check, not a proof.

How the other names offered compare: - "A deformation of convex projective structures": close. In the literature that phrase usually means shapes of whole surfaces built from these pieces; the dial itself is Benzécri's space. - Amari's α-family: a different dial. It changes the way you take straight lines on one fixed shape, not the shape. - Tropicalization / Maslov dequantization: names the temperature route only (cooling log-sum-exp into a max), not the whole dial.

Known versus ours. Known: Hilbert geometry, Vinberg's characteristic function, Benzécri's space, the Pick form and cubic differentials, Calabi's bound (Blaschke metric), homogeneity only at the ellipse and triangle, Thomas turn as hyperbolic area. Ours: reading Brennan's cubic-form dial as that space and the leftover turn as its curvature (Vinberg's metric); the numbers along the blend, trim and temperature routes; the cold-tail rate 1.45/β (numerical, not derived); the observation that the temperature dial is a route on the cubic-form dial, so the free-energy temperature and the Thomas turn are one dial reading. I found no source giving the curvature of the free-energy family; treat that as unchecked against the literature.

Leads, each judged on its own merits

  1. Relativity and Bayes as one rule on two shapes (section 5). Worth following. It explains why precession exists in a way our swap rule can use: the leftover turn is the area that roundness creates, and the flat simplex has none. The natural test is a dial between them: the free-energy bodies of Figure 8 run from round to simplex, so measure how the leftover turn of their Hilbert geometries shrinks as temperature drops. If it falls smoothly to zero, the temperature dial becomes a curvature dial, which would join the precession stream, the Maslov dial and the corner weights. If it doesn't, the idea ends there. Cheap to try. Tested in section 7: it fades smoothly (about 1.45/β when cold), so the lead stands. Next step on it: derive the 1.45 and see whether the turn field matches a swap-rule quantity.
  2. Stick-breaking is ∘₋₁ (section 1). Small but solid: it gives the cube-to-simplex map in our own operation, and the Dirichlet process (infinitely many cuts) becomes "∘₋₁ forever". Worth one look at whether the Chinese restaurant counting matches anything on the repetition dial; otherwise it is a clean restatement.
  3. e as the simplex's constant (section 4). Not a lead; it settles where e lives, which the hypersphere task can use.

Next (offered, not started)

  • Derive the cold-tail constant 1.45 in section 7 exactly, and repeat the cubic-form dial in three dimensions (ball to tetrahedron), where the in-between shapes are richer.
  • Lean (Mac Studio): S1 (stick-breaking total = fold of ∘₋₁), R1 (perturbation = ∘₁ on odds − 1), H2 (odds product = Einstein addition). All are short ring identities. From section 7, V3 (polar area of a disk = π/(1−|y|²)^{3/2}) is a clean calculus fact; the rest of section 7 is numerical and is not a Lean target.
